His father, also named Isaac, was a yeoman farmer and apothecary who later became a parish minister. Newton was the second of eight siblings. His mother, Hannah Ayscough, was a schoolteacher who passed on a love for learning to her children.

Newton’s formal education began at the local school but was interrupted by the Great Plague of London (1665-1666). Despite this, he pursued self-education through self-made textbooks and taught himself mathematics, including the rudiments of calculus, which would later be foundational to his seminal work on the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

After the plague subsided, Newton returned to Woolsthorpe to take over his father’s role as a schoolteacher. It was during this period, often described as the "Sombitarian era," that Newton’s scientific work began to take form. He became obsessed with the motion of the planets and stars, laying the groundwork for his later groundbreaking work on universal gravitation.

In 1665, Newton formulated his laws of motion and laws of universal gravitation. These monumental pieces of work laid the foundation for classical mechanics and formed the mathematical basis for modern physics. Newton’s law of universal gravitation, in particular, described how celestial bodies attract each other with an inverse square law, which remains the most accurate description of gravity known to science.

Newton’s contributions to science were not confined to mechanics. He made seminal contributions in optics, developing the theory of color and the prism experiment that demonstrated the spectrum of light, leading to his discoveries of white light as a combination of hues. Newton also made significant advancements in mathematics, particularly in the field of calculus.

In 1687, Newton published "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica" (Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), a groundbreaking work that transformed scientific understanding and laid the foundation for modern physics, chemistry, and astronomy. The book is often referred to as "the greatest single work in the history of science."

Newton’s death on 24 March 1727 did not come from natural causes; rather, he died from a severe bout of apoplexy while in the observatory at Cambridge, which he had rebuilt and greatly expanded that year.
